summaries.summary: Online discussions on social media platforms include offensive communications such as bullying, trolling, and harassment, causing psychological symptoms and motivating automatic detection using machine learning algorithms.
Detecting offensive language is challenging due to ambiguity and noisy social media language, and SemEval2019, Task 6 provided hierarchically annotated tweets with three sub-tasks.
The dataset had the following challenges.
Dataset was comparatively smaller.
Dataset was biased/imbalanced BIBREF3.
This paper proposes a comparative analysis for sub-task A :Offensive language identification of the SemEval2019, Task 6, which had total 104 team participation.

Prior offensive language research includes supervised classification, surveys, cyberbullying detection, GermEval 2018 with over 8,500 annotated tweets and maco-F1 score of 76.77%, and Aggression Identification with 15,000 annotated Facebook posts and comments and weighted F-score of 64%.
Data pre-processing is crucial before machine learning tasks because real time data could be noisy and unstructured, and tweets are pre-processed separately for the two models.
Pre-processing for Google model:
For the Google model, multiple #tags, multiple @symbols, and website links or urls are replaced with a single #tag, a single @-mention, and a single keyword URLS.
Pre-processing for fasttext model:
For the fasttext model, numbers, punctuation marks, urls, and symbols are removed, followed by NLTK tokenization, lowercasing, and NLTK stop word removal.
Word embeddings are ubiquitous for NLP because algorithms cannot process raw text, and they are vectors capturing semantic and contextual information of words.
FastText, created by Facebook BIBREF10, assumes words are character n-grams, provides vectors for out of vocabuary words, and is used here for token vectors of dimension 300 BIBREF11.
Universal Sentence Encoder, developed by Google, provides sentence-level embeddings of dimension 512 and generates a 512 length embedding vector for each tweet as classification features.
DMD, initially used in fluid dynamics and later applied for sentiment analysis, captures spatio-temporal features and motivated exploring DMD based features for this work.
Dynamic mode decomposition assumes evolution over a rectangular field is effected by a constant matrix $A$, whose dominant eignevalues and eigenvectors are used to understand system dynamics.
The pseudo inverse of ${\Phi }$ is used because $A$ is of rank m and ${\Phi }$ have m columns, and the columns of ${\Phi }$ are called DMD modes and form the features.

Time-lagged matrices are prepared as snapshots, and Eigensent BIBREF20 proposed HODMD for sentence embedings using word embeddings, with Fastext based embedding used to generate DMD and HODMD based features.
RKS approach proposed in BIBREF21, BIBREF22 explicitly maps data vectors to a space where linear separation is possible and provides an approximate kernel function via explicit mapping.
Here, $\phi (.)$ denotes the implicit mapping function, $Z(.)$ denotes the explicit mapping function using RKS, and ${\Omega _k}$ denotes random variable.
Figure FIGREF15 show the block diagram of the proposed approach.
OLID is a collection of English tweets collected using Twitter API with 14,460 annotated tweets, including train set 13,240 tweets and test set 860 tweets, with 14,100 tweets used here.
In Sub-task A: Offensive language identification, the goal was to discriminate offensive and not-offensive twitter posts, and team BIBREF3 obtained highest f1-score of 82.9%.
This section describes results as three cases, with Case 1 & 2 providing baselines for the proposed RKS approcah in case 3, and rank 1 achieved a maximum f1-score of 82.9%.
Case 1 uses Google universal encoder model, Fasttext, and DMD based features with several classifiers, and svm linear classifier and Logistic regression gave maximum accuracy of 82.44% and 82.56%.
For features generated by fasttext model, svm linear and logistic regression model have given maximum accuracies of 81.16% respectively.
Case 2 explores DMD based features, with HODMD order 2 & 3, SVM-linear kernel control parameter value 1000, and other values 0.1, 1, 100, 500, and 1000 tried.
Case 3 uses RKS to imporve evaluation scores by explicitly mapping embedding vectors to a linearly separable dimension, where regularized least-square based classification (RLSC) is performed.
For Google universal encoder model features with dimension 512 mapped to dimensions 100, 200, 500 and 1000 using RKS, the maximum accuracy obtained is 90.58% for higher dimension 1000.
For Fasttext model features mapped to dimensions 100, 200, 500 and 1000, the proposed method gave a maximum accuracy of 99.53%, with evaluation score improving as mapping dimension increases.

The current work uses SemEval 2019 shared task A data to compare Google universal sentence encoder, Fasttext based embedding, Dynamic Mode Decomposition based features, and RKS based explicit mapping approach, observing that RKS approach improved the results.
